questions.question: In Cricket, if the umpire extends both hands horizontally it means __________.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is** **__**wide ball.**__

__** [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] Key Points__**

__
 
• **Wide ball:-**

 
 
• **When the umpire extends both hands horizontally in cricket, it means that the ball has been declared a wide ball.**
 
• A wide ball is a delivery that is bowled** outside the batsman's reach and is not able to be hit by the batsman.**
 
• The umpire extends both hands horizontally to signal a wide ball to the **scorers and the players on the field.**
 
• This signal is recognized universally across all** cricket-playing nations.**
 
 

** [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] Additional Information__**

 
• **Dead ball:-**

 
 
• It is a ball that is not in play and cannot be hit by the batsman.
 
• It is usually declared by the umpire in case of an injury or when the ball gets stuck in the equipment of a fielder.
 
 
 
• ** No-ball:-**
 
 
• It​** **is a delivery that is bowled illegally, for instance, if the bowler oversteps the crease while bowling or if the delivery is above waist height.
 
• A no-ball results in the batting team getting an extra run and an additional ball to face.
 
 
 
• ** Run out:-**
 
 
• It **i**s a mode of dismissal in cricket when a batsman is out of his crease and a fielder throws the ball onto the stumps before the batsman can return to his crease.
 
• This can happen when the batsmen attempt to take a run or when the ball hits the bat and deflects onto the stumps.

questions.question: Since complete equality is impossible, the _____ of the Indian Constitution deals with the right to equality and equal protection of law subject to appropriate classification.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is__** अनुच्छेद 14.**__

__** [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] Key Points__**

__
 
• The Indian Constitution's emphasis on equality is related to Article 14, which guarantees equality before the law and equal protection of the law to all persons within the territory of India.
 
• Article 14
 
 
• Article 14 of the Indian Constitution is about 'Equality Before Law' and it states:
 
• "The State shall not deny to any person equality before the law or the equal protection of the laws within the territory of India."
 
• This article is a fundamental right under Part III of the Constitution of India, which talks about Rights to Equality.
 
• The principle of 'Equality before law' is of British origin, while 'Equal protection of the laws' is borrowed from the Constitution of the United States.
 
 
 
• 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 

 
 

 **Article 15**
 
 
Article 15 prohibits discrimination by the state against any citizen on grounds only of caste, religion, sex, race, and place of birth.

 
Fundamental rights are provided to every citizen of the country without any discrimination.

 
These rights entitle an individual to live life with dignity.

 
 
 

 **Article 16**
 
 
Article 16 of the Indian Constitution guarantees equal opportunity to all citizens in matters related to employment in the public sector.

 
The provision of equality is only applicable to the employment or offices which are held by the State.

 
The State is still free to lay down the requisite qualifications for the recruitment of employees for the Government services.

 
 
 

 **Article 13**
 
 
 
• Article 13 deals with Laws Inconsistent with Fundamental Rights.
 
• Article 13 declares that all laws that are inconsistent with or in derogation of any of the fundamental rights shall be void.
 
• It expressively provides for the doctrine of judicial review.
 
• This power has been conferred on the Supreme Court (Article 32) and the high courts (Article 226) that can declare a law unconstitutional and invalid on the ground of contravention of any of the Fundamental Rights.

questions.question: Which Indian state is renowned for the traditional canal irrigation method known as 'Kulh'?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __Himachal Pradesh__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__** 

__
 
• Kulhs:-

 
 
• 'Kulh' is the most common source of irrigation in the hilly state of Himachal Pradesh.
 
• These​ are small local irrigation canals found in Himachal Pradesh.
 
• They are mainly found in hilly/mountainous regions where they are used to transport melted water from glaciers to villages due to the effect of gravity.
 
• Under this system, water from the streams is diverted into man-made channels that carry this water to various villages.
 
• They serve as a source of canal irrigation for agricultural crops.
 
• Being a hilly area, it was not possible to build tube-wells, borewells in Himachal Pradesh. That's why 'kulhs' came into existence.
 
• They are jointly managed by common neighboring villages.
 
• As of today, most of them are defunct after being taken over by the Irrigation Department.
 
• They are water channels most commonly found in mountain areas. 
 
• Kulhs of Himachal Pradesh

• Kerela - *Surangams*
 
• Karnataka - *Kattas*

• Madhya Pradesh and Uttar Pradesh - *Bundhis*

questions.question: Following are the industry categories classified under the Industrial Policy Resolution 1956, EXCEPT:

options.text: industries with public sector taking the lead and the private sector playing a supplementary role
industries with exclusive ownership of the state

questions.solution:
The correct answer is__** industries in the cooperative sector.**__

__** [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] Key Points__**

__
 
• **Industrial Policy Resolution 1956:-**

 
 
• **It was a policy framework for the development of industries in India.**
 
• The policy classified industries into three categories: (1) industries in the private sector, (2) industries with the public sector taking the lead and the private sector playing a supplementary role, and (3) industries with exclusive ownership of the state.
 
• The** policy did not include industries in the cooperative sector** as a separate category.
 
• The cooperative sector refers to businesses that are owned and operated by **a group of individuals who share the profits and control the operations.**
 
• ** The Industrial Policy Resolution of 1956 was replaced by the New Industrial Policy in 1991, which encouraged liberalization, privatization, and globalization of industries in India.**
 
• **Highlights of IPR 1956:**
 
 
• In order to initiate a new industry or expand existing capacity, private entrepreneurs were supposed to obtain licenses from the government.
 
• Licensing, imposition of the tax, tax exemptions, and subsidies were used by the government:
 
 
• to regulate private industries.
 
• bring about a reduction in regional disparities in industrial development. 
 
• to keep a check on the production of goods that are socially undesirable.
 
 
 
 
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Industries with public sector taking the lead and the private sector playing a supplementary role:-**

 
 
• It refers to industries where the government takes the lead in ownership and management, and the private sector plays a supportive role.
 
• This model was adopted for industries such as steel, coal, and power generation.
 
 
 
• **Industries in the private sector:-**
 
 
• It refers to industries that are owned and operated by private individuals or companies. This model was encouraged for industries such as consumer goods, textiles, and services.
 
 
 
• **Industries with exclusive ownership of the state:-**
 
 
• It refers to industries that are wholly owned and operated by the state. This model was adopted for industries such as defense, atomic energy, and railways.

questions.question: Pola festival is associated with which of the following states?

__
 
• Pola Festival

 
 
• Pola Festival is a thanksgiving festival celebrated by farmers in Maharashtra and Chhattisgarh, to acknowledge the importance of bulls and oxen, who are a crucial part of agriculture and farming activities.
 
• It falls on the day of the Pithori Amavasya in the month of Shraavana.
 
• The farmers decorate their bulls on this day and then worship them to perform in the festival.
 
• This festival is celebrated to show their gratitude towards the bulls for their assistance in the agricultural works by the farmers.
 
• On the following day of the festival, the plowing activities are started and seeds are sown in the fields.
 
• It is a very unique festival in Maharashtra where an animal is made the focus of the occasion.
 
• During the Sravana month, the Pola festival is celebrated on a new moon day which is also called the Pithori Amavasya day.
 
• The farmers celebrate this day with many traditional dishes like kunbis, poli and karanji which are authentic Maharashtra dishes.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

• **Nagaland:-**
 
 
• **​**It celebrates the** Hornbill festival** in December to showcase the state's tribal culture and traditions.
 
 
 
• ** Karnataka:-**
 
 
• **​**It is famous for its **Mysuru Dasara festival,** which is a 10-day-long celebration of the victory of good over evil.

questions.question: The original Constitution of India was hand written in English by:
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __Prem Behari Narain Raizada.__ 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Constitution of India:-

 
 
• It​ is a written set of rules that governs any state.
 
• The Constitution was partialy enacted on 26th November 1949 and completely it came into force on 26 January 1950.
 
• The Constitution was drafted by the Constituent Assembly which comprised of the indirectly elected members along with the nominated members.
 
• The Original Constitution in the English language was written by Prem Bihari Narain Raizada
 
• The Consitution in Hindi was written by another calligrapher Vasant Krishna Vaidya.
 
• Raizada was born in a family of calligraphers in the year 1901 and he died in the year 1966.
 
• Raizada did not charge a single penny for writing the Constitution instead, he wrote his name along with his grandfather's name at the bottom of every page of the Constitution.
 
• The Constitution at the time of its inception consisted of 395 articles, 22 parts, and 8 Schedules.
 
• At present, this document consists of about 448 articles, 25 parts and 12 schedules.
 
• There have been 105 amendments in the Constitution of India up to October 2021.
 
• The first amendment was done in 1951.
 After that, the Constitution has been amended 104 times.
 
• This is the beauty of the Indian Constitution.
 
• The Constituent Assembly took almost 2years, 11 months, and 18 days to complete the task of drafting this historic document.
 
• There were a total of 11 sessions of the Constituent Assembly during this period.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

Some Recent Amendments made in the Constitution are as follows:

 
 

 **Amendment number and year**
 **The subject of the Amendment**
 
 

 99th Amendment (2014)
 Provision of National Judicial Appointment Commission
 
 

 100th Amendment (2015)
 Land Boundary Agreement between India and Bangladesh
 
 

 101st Amendment (2016)
 Introduction of the Goods and Service (GST) Act in the country
 
 

 102nd Amendment (2018)
 Constitutional status to National Commission for Backward Classes.
 
 

 103rd Amendment (2019)
 Provision of 10% Reservation for Economically Weaker Sections (EWS)
 
 

 104th Amendment (2020)
 Extension of the reservation of seats for SCs and STs in the Lok Sabha and States Assemblies. It removed the reserved seats for the Anglo-Indian community in the Lok Sabha and state assemblies.

questions.question: Who described in 1662 that when a gas was pumped into an enclosed space, it would shrink to fit in that space, but the pressure exerted by the gas on the container would increase?
questions.solution:

__
 
• ** Robert Boyle:-**

 
 
• He studied the behaviour of gases enclosed in a chamber and formulated the gas law named after him.
 
• He also contributed to physiology and to the founding of modern chemistry. 
 
• He was the first to isolate and characterize gases like nitric oxide, hydrogen chloride, ammonia, and oxygen.
 
• He helped to establish the experimental method in chemistry. Boyle introduced many new ways of identifying the chemical composition of substances. 
 
 
 
• ​Law of Behaviour of Gases: These laws tell us about the behaviour of gases. By that, we mean the values and relations of temperature, pressure, and volume, etc.
 
• Boyle’s Law:- 
 
 
• Suppose you have some Helium in a gas container at low pressure and temperature. if you increase the volume of the container at a constant temperature, the pressure of the gas will decrease.
 
• ** Boyle’s law can be stated as the volume (V) is inversely proportional to pressure (P) at a constant temperature.**
 
 

**Addᵢₜᵢₒₙₐₗ Iₙfₒᵣₘₐₜᵢₒₙ__**

 
• ** Jacques Charles;-**

 
 
• He​ is known for Charles's Law, which describes the relationship between **gas volume and temperature at a constant pressure.**
 
 
 
• ** Joseph Gay Lussac:-**
 
 
• He​ is known for Gay-Lussac's Law, which describes the relationship between **gas pressure and temperature at a constant volume. **
 
 
 
• **Amedeo Avogadro:-**

questions.question: Which of the following Articles of the Indian Constitution mentions the right to form co-operative societies?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**19 (1) (c).**__ [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The 97th Constitutional Amendment Act of 2011 gave constitutional status and protection to cooperative societies.
 
• In this context, it made the following three changes in the Constitution:
 
 
• It made the right to form cooperative societies a fundamental right (Article 19).
 
• It included a new Directive Principle of State Policy on the promotion of cooperative societies (Article 43-B).
 
• It added a new Part IX-B in the Constitution which is entitled “The Cooperative Societies” (Articles 243-ZH to 243-ZT).
 
 
 
• The new Part IX-B contains various provisions to ensure that the cooperative societies in the country function in a democratic, professional, autonomous, and economically sound manner.
 
• It empowers the Parliament in respect of multi-state cooperative societies and the state legislatures in respect of other cooperative societies to make the appropriate law.
 
• Article 43B deals with the promotion of cooperative societies. The State shall endeavor to promote voluntary formation, autonomous functioning, democratic control, and professional management of co-operative societies. [Article 43B Inserted by the 97th Constitution Amendment Act, 2011].

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• 97th Amendment Act, 2011

 
 
• The right to form cooperative societies is a fundamental right that has been provided in the Indian Constitution.
 
• It is enshrined in Article 19(c) of the Constitution, which guarantees the freedom to form associations or unions.
 
• This right was added to the Constitution by the 97th Amendment Act of 2011.
 
• Article 19(1)(c) guarantees all citizens the right "to form associations or unions or co-operative societies".
 
• However, this right, like other rights under Article 19, is not absolute and is subject to reasonable restrictions under clause (4) of the same article, namely "in the interests of the sovereignty and integrity of India, the security of the State, friendly relations with foreign States, public order or morality or in relation to contempt of court, defamation or incitement to an offence".

questions.question: Who started the practice of celebrating Nauroz during the Delhi Sultanate period?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Ghiyasuddin Balban.**__

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Ghiyasuddin Balban:-**

 
 
• **He started the practice of celebrating Nauroz during the Delhi Sultanate period.**
 
• Ghiyasuddin Balban was a powerful ruler of the Delhi Sultanate who reigned from 1266 to 1287 AD.
 
• He is credited with introducing many administrative and military reforms during his reign.
 
 
 
• **Nauroz:-**
 
 
• It is a Persian term that means "new day" and is celebrated on the first day of spring.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Sikandar Sur:-**

 
 
• He was not a ruler of the Delhi Sultanate period.
 
• He was a ruler of the Sur dynasty that ruled over parts of India from 1540 to 1556 AD.
 
 
 
• **Shamsuddin Iltutmish:-**
 
 
• He was a ruler of the Delhi Sultanate period who reigned from 1211 to 1236 AD.
 
• However, there is no historical evidence to suggest that he started the practice of celebrating Nauroz.
 
 
 
• **Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq:-**
 
 
• He was a ruler of the Tughlaq dynasty that ruled over parts of India from 1320 to 1325 AD. He also did not start the practice of celebrating Nauroz during the Delhi Sultanate period.

The correct answer is __**Mool Chand Garg.**__

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

 
• **Mool Chand Garg:-**

 
 
• **He heads the Print and Digital Media Association (PADMA).**
 
• Mool Chand Garg is a veteran journalist and media executive with over 35 years of experience in the industry.
 
• He has worked with leading media organizations such as Zee News, Sahara News, and Dainik Bhaskar.
 
• As the head of PADMA, Garg is responsible for ensuring that member publishers adhere to the code of ethics and guidelines set by the organization.
 
• This includes maintaining editorial independence, accuracy, and fairness in reporting.
 
 
 
• **PADMA:-**
 
 
• It is a self-regulatory body approved by the Central Government for publishers of news and current affairs across the country.

questions.question: In which year was the first railway line constructed in India?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**1853**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Railway in India:-**

 
 
• **The first railway line in India was constructed in the year 1853, between Bombay (now Mumbai) and Thane.**
 
• The line was constructed by the Great Indian Peninsula Railway (GIPR) under the British East India Company's rule.
 
• The 34 km long railway line was opened for public use on 16th April 1853, and it was a major milestone in the history of Indian transportation.
 
• The first train that ran on this line was named 'The Sahib', and it had three steam locomotives named 'Sindh', 'Sultan', and 'Sahib'.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• 1887 was the year when the first electric tramway was introduced in India, in the city of Bombay.
 
• 1890 represents the year when the first railway line was constructed in the state of Madras (now Chennai) by the Madras Railway Company, connecting the port city of Madras with the inland town of Arcot.

questions.question: All of the following reasons can be attributed to the lack of access to credit for the poor EXCEPT:

options.text: lack of stable source of income
lenders prefer dealing in large loans in small numbers to minimise administration costs
absence of collateral with clear title

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**low information monitoring costs.**__

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

 
• **Lack of access to credit for the poor:-**

 
 
• It is a pervasive problem in many developing countries, and it can be attributed to various factors.
 
 
 
• One of the main reasons is the lack of a stable source of income, which makes it difficult for lenders to assess the creditworthiness of the borrower and increases the risk of default.
 
• Another reason is the absence of collateral with clear title, which makes it difficult for lenders to secure their loans and reduces their willingness to lend to poor borrowers.
 
• Lenders may also prefer dealing in large loans in small numbers to minimize administration costs, which can make it difficult for poor borrowers who need small loans to access credit.
 
• However, low information monitoring costs are not a reason for the lack of access to credit for the poor. In fact, low monitoring costs can make it easier for lenders to monitor the use of the loan and reduce the risk of default.

questions.question:
Which of the following is an example of capital receipt?

A) Borrowings from World Bank to fund Project to Save Tigers

B) Sale of 30% stake in a PSU to private companies
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Both A and B.**__

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

 
• **Capital receipt:-**

 
 
• It refers to the inflow of funds that are not generated from the regular operations of a business or organization.
 
• It can include sources such as sale of assets, borrowing, or capital contributions from shareholders or investors.
 
• Borrowings from World Bank to fund Project to Save Tigers - This is a capital receipt because it increases a liability (the amount borrowed needs to be repaid) and is intended for a capital project (funding a specific conservation project).
 
• Sale of 30% stake in a PSU to private companies is an example of capital receipt, as it is an inflow of funds from the sale of an asset.
